implementation_notes: Rust replaces the class-static accessor with a type that cannot be written twice: a static OnceLock<Config> plus get_or_init gives a lazily published, thread-safe singleton with no unsafe code, and LazyLock (1.80) shortens the common case to a deref. Before 1.70 the once_cell crate provided the same types, with once_cell::sync::Lazy as the macro-free lazy_static replacement. The cells are Send/Sync-checked, so sole ownership and publication are compiler-enforced; where a composition root can create the value, passing &Config down still beats a global static.
pitfalls: OnceLock is never poisoned on panic, but LazyLock is: a panicking initialiser makes every later access panic, so shared globals need panic-free initialisers.
Static values are never dropped: sockets, file handles and other resources held by the singleton are released only at process exit, and tooling may report the allocation as a leak.
Uniqueness is per linked copy of the static: a cdylib loaded twice, or a test binary, holds its own instance.
Tests run in parallel in one process and share the static, so state leaks across tests unless the value is injected or globals are avoided in library code.

variants.name: std::sync::LazyLock (deref-initialised global)
variants.implementation_notes: LazyLock is the shorter form when one closure defines the value: the static derefs to &T and initialises on first use, so access sites need no get_or_init call. It cannot take extra inputs after LazyLock::new (unlike OnceLock, which accepts a fresh closure per get_or_init call), and a panicking initialiser poisons the value permanently - pick OnceLock when the initialiser can fail, needs runtime arguments, or when the value may be set from main.
pitfalls: A panicking LazyLock initialiser poisons the value: every later deref panics with the same cause.
Initialisation happens at the first deref, which can be inside a hot path - keep the closure cheap or force it during startup with LazyLock::force.
Statics are not dropped, so a LazyLock<T> holding a Drop type releases nothing at exit.

variants.name: once_cell crate (pre-1.70 toolchains)
variants.implementation_notes: For toolchains older than Rust 1.70, or code that still uses the pre-std idioms, the once_cell crate provides the same machinery: sync::OnceCell with get_or_init, or sync::Lazy as the macro-free lazy_static replacement; the crate documents that most of its functionality moved into std with 1.70. The trade is a dependency plus the same non-dropping static lifetime - migrate to OnceLock/LazyLock when the MSRV allows it.
pitfalls: Declare the holder as static, not const: a const Lazy is a fresh value on every use and silently initialises repeatedly.
The crate is unnecessary once the MSRV reaches 1.70 (OnceLock) or 1.80 (LazyLock); carrying both vocabularies in one codebase is the real cost.
Statics holding the crate's Lazy release nothing at exit either.
